p: Yes, like many New Yorkers, I have... (CROSS-TALK)

Right. Why should New Yorkers believe that you can independently act

when it comes to being a DOI Commissioner, with these loose relationships with the administration—or with the Mayor?

Because that is what I have done throughout my career. I've acted with integrity and independence as a federal prosecutor. I've investigated people I've supported in the past. It has no bearing and will have no bearing on how I conduct myself in this position, should I be confirmed.

Okay. And given your previous relationship with the Mayor, would you commit, on the record, to recusing yourself from any investigation that directly involves the Mayor or any senior mayoral official?
I will commit to seeking the advice of counsel regarding recusal and following the advice I receive.
Okay. Do you believe that your prior financial support of the Mayor creates a conflict of interest in this role?
I... (CROSS-TALK)
And if not, why not?
Yes, I...
Yeah.
I do not actually...
Okay.
(INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)
Okay, and why not?

Because I have approached-- it is within my very being to approach every investigation based on the evidence, facts, and the law, and nothing else. That is how I have conducted myself throughout my 20-year legal career. And that is how I would conduct myself here. Nevertheless, if any such situation arises, I will seek the advice of counsel. And I will follow any recusal advice I receive.

All right, thank you. Thank you for that response. DOI is supposed to be independent and hold the City government accountable. Can you point to a time in your career where you have challenged leadership or authority, despite political pressure? And this could include workplace-related political pressure.

So I think I mentioned that I led an investigation of sexual abuse of female

inmates at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. As federal prosecutors, we regularly interacted with law enforcement officers who worked at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn as part of our other investigations and cases. They certainly were very interested in the investigation I was conducting. They wanted it to finish quickly and to move forward as quickly as possible, and often sought information about the investigation. And I blocked all of that out and conducted the investigation, taking the time it needed to conduct by following the evidence and the law.
If DOI uncovers a wrongdoing within the Mayor’s Office, are you prepared to pursue that fully, even if it puts you at odds with the administration?
Absolutely... (CROSS-TALK)
The administration that appointed you?
Absolutely.

And, we have seen high-profile corruption issues in government, at multiple levels, including here in New York City. Why

should the public trust that the DOI, under your leadership, will not be influenced by politics?

Again, because that is how I have conducted myself throughout my 20-year legal career. The importance of independence and integrity of investigations at DOI is of the utmost importance to me. It is how I will lead DOI if confirmed. It is how DOI has operated, with its amazing staff, doing amazing work under difficult circumstances. And it is how I would continue to lead

Thank you. I just want to dive into some NYCHA concerns and questions I have. I chair the Public Housing Committee, and during my time in office, NYCHA has experienced repeated instances of corruption, including procurement irregularities, bribery schemes, and failures of internal oversight. Given your background in public integrity and complex corruption investigations, how would you approach the oversight of an agency as large and as complex as NYCHA?

Thank you for the question. My understanding is that DOI currently has a squad dedicated to investigating issues at NYCHA, and I

certainly would continue to have a squad dedicated solely to that. I think one of my first orders of business after becoming commissioner, should I be confirmed, would be to assess the needs and capabilities of all the squads, including that one, and try to understand if there are additional resources they need, and if so, how we can get them what they need. So really, I think the first few months I'm at DOI will be about listening, learning, and then making informed decisions about how to improve things as necessary.

Okay, thank you. NYCHA is subject to federal oversight and ongoing monitorship. How would you ensure that the Department of Investigation asserts its authority and fulfills its mandate without duplicating federal efforts or deferring to heavily federalized partners?

So, I think open lines of communication are important, knowing what the federal monitor is looking into, because we don't want to duplicate efforts, particularly given the limited resources of the department.

I also think certain things that the federal monitor looks into, which may be more systemic issues, can potentially inform investigations that the DOI conducts. So if they find that there's, you know, a systemic issue with a certain area, there may be then room for a DOI investigation about individual misconduct in that area. And that's certainly a way that those two entities can inform one another.

Okay. And you've led investigations involving the entrenched systems of abuse and corruption where misconduct was allowed to persist for years. What specific lessons from those experiences would you bring to DOI’s oversight over NYCHA?

I think one thing I've learned is that sometimes well-meaning policies can really result in systemic institutional failures. So I think it's important to look at what the goal was, what the actual policy is, and then how that's been implemented. And you may start out with a great goal and still end up with a systemic failure. And so you have to look at each stage of the process.

Thank you. Many NYCHA employees and residents report fear of retaliation for raising concerns. How would you ensure that DOI is viewed as safe, trusted-- a safe and trusted venue for reporting this type of misconduct?

I think a lot of it is making the public aware, frankly, of DOI's existence. I'm not sure that the general public, including NYCHA residents, necessarily know about DOI or what it does. So I think there have to be outreach efforts to ensure that communities that have things to report are reached out to and know what DOI does, know that it's independent, and can feel comfortable, and then also know about the whistleblower protections available.

And according to a report by Tim McNichols (phonetic), complaints about NYCHA submitted to the New York State Department of Investigation have steadily increased. In recent years, approximately 1,700 complaints were made in 2022, approximately 2,500 in 2023, and 3,300 in 2024. Given the significant increase in NYCHA's related complaints to DOI, how would you ensure that

these reports lead to meaningful systemic change and improved conditions for residents rather than remaining limited to a reactive investigations?

So I think I would focus on two areas in trying to address that, which is obviously a very concerning upward trend in complaints. I think the first is making sure that policy recommendations that have already been made and accepted are, in fact, implemented. So I think follow-up is very, very important, and that's something I would prioritize. I also think that there should be some analysis of the types of complaints received and to see what areas they fall in as a predictor of where DOI should be putting its resources. So, you know, if there are complaints about a certain area, then that is an area that DOI should consider proactively investigating rather than waiting for, you know, a particular individual complaint to come into the DOI complaint system to address it.

All Right. And my last question—last week, Leader Jeffries, Council Member Mealy, and I were in Brownsville to announce $1 million in funding for

security cameras and infrastructure upgrades at three NYCHA developments, including $250,000 for Carter G Woodson Houses, which is in my district. This is a development with a tragic history. Several years ago, a handyman murdered three senior residents. Last year, I led the effort to restore, along with my colleagues, $7 million in funding for a NYCHA security guard program at about 55 NYCHA developments after it was proposed for elimination in the City's budget. However, in 2025, in an investigation report by an online publication, the City found that security and fire guards at NYCHA developments were frequently absent from their posts and, in some cases, falsified timesheets, putting residents at risk. As the nominee for DOI Commissioner, how would you ensure stronger oversight and accountability of NYCHA security contracts so that resources the City fights to preserve actually result in a real on-the-ground safety for residents?

So I think the City's reporting on those issues was actually based on a DOI investigation and findings made by DOI. So I think

the good news is that DOI has already been focused on this area.
Right.

And they issued recommendations. So what I would do as DOI Commissioner is to ensure that the recommendations that have been accepted by NYCHA are, in fact, being implemented, and follow up regularly on that.
All right. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. We have also been joined by Council Member Krishnan, and I will turn it over to him for questions.

Thank you, Chair. Good to see you, Ms. Shihata, and thank you for your testimony today, too. I wanted to ask some questions in a few different areas and just clarify a few things. So, just taking a step back, you've testified on a number of different topics at this point, too, but what would you say would be your top priorities as Commissioner to improve the functioning of the agency itself?
I think the top priority is ensuring that DOI has the resources and budget it needs to conduct its mission.

And I would agree with that, too. And I think that has been a major issue. One question, I know Council Member Lee asked a bit about the budget deficit now and the need to increase resources for DOI, which has been a big issue. Can you talk a bit more first, just about where you see there being a need for resources within DOI? What particular staffing would you need, and how would that help with the investigations you have to?

Sure. I think one area where, based on my conversations with people at DOI, there has been significant turnover has been with investigators. So I think that's a particular area where I would focus on getting resources so that we could hire sufficient investigators and then retain them, ensuring there is a path for career development for those people. I think often why people leave jobs like that is because they have opportunities for greater

compensation, not only in the private sector but sometimes even within city government, and maybe don't see a path for career development. I know the prior commissioner worked on these issues and focused on them intensely, and I would intend to continue that.

And part of that issue, I think, is sort of looking at, again, the way in which DOI, as you might be aware of too, is reliant particularly on asset forfeiture from one case in particular, but could be other ones as well. Which, as we saw in our budget hearings earlier this year, too, ended up funding a number of core, while new, core new operations within the agency. And frankly, an agency like this should not be so dependent on asset forfeiture to continue funding new but still critical operations of the agency. What do you think about the role of asset forfeiture funds? How would you work to ensure that the agency has the resources it needs and is not depending on asset forfeiture in one case in particular, as the way to fund the agency?

So my understanding is that there are particular rules that govern how you can

use asset forfeiture funds and that, as a general matter, they are supposed to supplement budgetary needs for the department, but not supplant them. I think it's very important that DOI ensures it's following any Department of Justice rules regarding asset forfeiture and any state rules regarding asset forfeiture, so as not to jeopardize the ability to continue receiving and using asset forfeiture. So I think that needs to be looked at very carefully. And I think again, I plan to be a relentless advocate for DOI’s budget and to ensure that the Mayor's Office, the City Council, and the public at large really understand what's at stake here when the department is not funded properly.

Do you think there's also a role-- there's been more conversations and similar investigative agencies across the country, that are funded budgetarily by a percentage of the city budget to preserve its independence, so it's not going up and down depending on the political or administrative whims or budget deficits. Are you open to-- do you see a role in considering ‘PEG-ing’ DOI's funding to a percentage of the City budget, as

opposed to the budget, financial, or political whims of a given moment?

I think that is certainly one way to ensure DOI's independence and also the appearance of its independence. And I believe you're correct that other cities have followed that model. My understanding is that the prior DOI commissioner supported just such a proposal in the City Charter revision process, and I'm certainly open to considering that.

Shifting gears, in December, the DOI published a report that criticized the Conflict of Interest Board for allowing city attorneys to represent other clients without obtaining a formal written waiver that would result in the publication of a formal written opinion. The report criticized the Conflicts of Interest Board for not making redacted advisory opinions available to the public as required by law. COIB maintains that they have not done anything wrong. What remedy would you recommend when there's a disagreement between DOI and COIB about the

interpretation of laws governing the Conflicts of Interest Board?

So DOI doesn't have the power to force agencies to implement or accept its determinations, but it can make them public, as DOI has done here. I think there may also be a role to play for the City's Corporation Counsel to weigh in on the issue and give a definitive opinion about it.

Now, another issue that's come up and you've heard too is--let me see, is the fact that the importance of the independence of this role, as I'm sure you know well and can agree to, and in particular, making sure that this role in the Department of Investigation, while the nomination comes from City Hall, that there is a clear wall of independence between DOI, City Hall, and frankly every agency in city government. And you've heard a number of questions to this point already, really going to the fact that you know, I think all of us, and in particular, think that the independence of this office is sacred. And you know, I think given your time as the federal prosecutor as well, the federal restrictions like the Hatch Act are very clear about ways in which to

preserve the independence of federal prosecutors when it comes to their work in the federal government. So, given all that's been asked about as well, what concrete measures would you also put in place to ensure that there is clear independence between the DOI, every agency, including City Hall as well?

I think the key is investigative independence, that we are not-- DOI is not providing details or specifics about ongoing investigations to anyone. In certain contexts, there are things like grand jury secrecy laws that legally prevent any such information sharing from occurring, but that, as a general matter, should go beyond just those types of investigations and grand jury concerns. I think you ensure independence of investigations by having confidentiality. It protects the investigation, and it protects independent decision-making.

I think to your point too, and as you mentioned as well, you know, preserving that independence becomes so important. I'm sure you can agree, given the last four years as well, the incredible work that DOI did, too, which

resulted in the federal cases that came forward as well, just speaks to how important it is to have that independence. So your consideration, thought, and testimony in support of preserving the independence of that office, too, is critical, I think. And it highlights one of the main roles that DOI needs to ensure it plays as it moves forward in city government. Another question I have as well is, uh, you heard from Council Member Banks a bit about-- with respect to NYCHA, the way in which DOI can play a role in continuing both building on the federal consent decree, but also working separately and apart from that too. How do you take that lens to fighting corruption and conflict of interest across all city agencies? How would you ensure proactively that DOI is fulfilling its mandate to root out waste and, frankly, corruption and conflicts of interest at all city agencies in addition to NYCHA?

I think it's very important that DOI is looking at ways to find the systemic risks in various areas and agencies.

I think part of that can be gleaned from past investigations that the DOI has done—making sure, not just being focused on particular findings in a particular investigation, but then stepping back and taking a broader view to see what broader lessons can be learned that can apply not just to that agency but to other agencies as well—potentially issuing a formal report about that and publicizing it, and obviously engaging with agency heads to ensure that they are not just aware of DOI's findings, but implementing them and implementing recommendations—and also being proactively engaged in understanding why certain recommendations have not been implemented and seeing if there's, you know, workarounds to that. Sometimes it may be funding issues, but sometimes it may be the practicality of the recommendation. And if that's the issue, then I think DOI should be proactively trying to address that because the goal here is prevention as much as possible. That is better for everybody involved, including the taxpayers. So, I think it's important to look at ways we can do that, which may involve data analytics. One of the things I'm interested in

doing when I get there is understanding what DOI is already doing in that regard and seeing how that can be enhanced.

I think prevention is a key point as well. We've seen from the last four years, across city agencies, it's a lot, as you know well, it's a lot of work after the fact to correct an issue—corrective action plans, and ensure that whether it's violations of sanctuary laws that have happened—that after the fact we were trying to remedy—and we had a hearing about that earlier this year in the Oversight Committee—we all benefit from having preventative measures in place and protections to ensure that violations of the law by agencies or corruption are not ongoing. So I think the more that DOI can take that role, the better it is for the efficiency of government overall, too. Finally, in the past, advocates have requested that community input be taken into consideration when appointing Inspectors General, particularly the NYPD Inspector General. Are you open to such input? How would you solicit, if you are open

to that input, public participation in the selection process here?

I am open to that input. I think I would need to understand how that input in the past has been received before expounding on exactly what that might look like. But as a general matter, I think the Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD should have relationships with key stakeholders, including advocates in that area. That includes receiving input regarding who or what qualifications would be ideal for a person in that position.
Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you. And seeing no other members have questions, Ms. Shihata, you are excused.
Thank you.

I now open up the floor to the public for comment. We ask that you please limit your comments to two minutes. If you wish to speak, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant of Arms, and you'll be given the opportunity to make your comments. Also, if you have a written

statement, please provide a copy of the statement to the Sergeant of Arms. I first called Ms. Maria Cruz Melendez and Ms. Kristen Mace.

Good morning, Madam Chair, and Members of the Committee. My name is Maria Cruz Melendez, and I'm a partner at the law firm Skadden, Arps in New York City. Prior to that, I served for over a decade as an Assistant United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, where, among other things, I served as Deputy Chief of the Public Integrity Section and Deputy Chief of the Civil Rights Section. I greatly appreciate the opportunity to speak before you today in strong support of the nomination of Nadia Shihata to serve as Commissioner of the Department of Investigation. During the entirety of my tenure at the EDNY, I had the pleasure of working alongside Nadia, and I know her to be an attorney of exceptional integrity and judgment with a true dedication to public service. At EDNY, we worked together on various matters, including as trial partners, and I saw

firsthand her skills as an investigator and advocate, as well as her abilities in managing complex, high-stakes matters with rigor and fairness. As you're aware, Nadia held multiple leadership roles at EDNY involving organized crime, corruption, and civil rights. And in each of her positions, she demonstrated not only legal expertise but also a strong moral compass and a commitment to doing what is right. She also earned the respect of her peers, direct reports, and law enforcement partners due to her professionalism and approach to leadership. Nadia works tirelessly, approaching every case with care and precision, and she's deeply committed to achieving justice for victims, while at the same time bringing compassion and sound judgment to her work—attributes that are essential for leading an agency charged with maintaining accountability and public trust. Having myself investigated and prosecuted cases together with DOI, I recognize that it is an agency that requires independence, integrity, and unwavering commitment to the rule of law. (TIMER) Nadia embodies all of these qualities. I'm confident

that if confirmed, she will serve with distinction and uphold the highest standards of this office. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good morning. My name is Kristen Mace, and I'm currently a partner at the law firm of Covington and Burling. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak today. It is my honor to offer my unequivocal support for the nomination of Nadia Shihata for Commissioner of the New York City Department of Investigation. I previously served alongside Nadia Shihata in the US Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. Nadia and I joined the US Attorney's Office in the same year, I believe it was 2011, and I had the honor of working with Nadia for more than a decade. During the latter part of that period, I served as Chief of the Criminal Division for the US Attorney's Office and was responsible for the supervision of all of the criminal investigations and prosecutions of the office, including Nadia's work in the areas of anti-corruption and combating the

victimization of vulnerable individuals and communities. Nadia's exacting preparation, tireless dedication, fearless perseverance, and fairness made her the model of what every citizen would want from a prosecutor and a public servant. She made tough cases and refused to be intimidated or deterred from the mission. But she also approached every individual, victim, witness, target, or criminal defendant with the utmost independence and professionalism, and she has always treated everyone with dignity and fairness. Even as Chief of the Criminal Division, I often sought out Nadia's counsel and advice. She's an exceptional strategic thinker and an accomplished advocate, but more importantly, she was never distracted from the goal by any type of influence or bias. I appreciated Nadia's counsel so much because she is an independent thinker who stays clear-eyed about the mission with a focus on the best way to reach a just result and make New York City safer and fairer for all.

I have never seen Nadia express or act from bias. I have always known her to make independent decisions based on the facts and the law alone. As a lawyer, and more importantly, as a citizen of New York City, (TIMER) I'm delighted... May I just finish? Thank you. I'm delighted to know that if confirmed, Nadia Shihata will be in a position to hold our public officials to the highest ethical standards and that if anyone strays from his or her duty, she will fight to address a problem, ensure a just result, and recommend necessary improvements. I am confident that Nadia Shihata will be one of the most effective commissioners New York City has ever had. Thank you very much.

The George Washington University Law School 2000 H Street NW | Washington, DC 20052 e: Kristin.Johnson@law.gwu.edu April 14, 2026 The Honorable Julie Menin, Speaker The Honorable Dr. Nantasha Williams, Deputy Speaker The Honorable Sandra Ung, Chair, Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards and Ethics Elected Members New York City Council 250 Broadway New York, NY 10007 Subject: Commendation in Support of Nadia Shihata, Nominee for Commissioner of the Department of Investigation To the Honorable Julie Menon, Speaker; Dr. Nantasha Williams, Deputy Speaker; the Honorable Sandra Ung, Chair, Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards and Ethics; and Members of the New York City Council: I write in support of Ms. Nadia Shihata’s nomination to serve as Commissioner of the Department of Investigation (DOI) for the City of New York. I have known Ms. Shihata for over twenty years and can unequivocally attest that she has a demonstrated track record of executing her duties as a federal prosecutor and lawyer in private practice exceptionally well and without fear or favor. These skills will enable her to effectively lead the DOI as the agency that investigates and exposes corruption, waste, and fraud in City government; prevents future misconduct by proposing policy and procedural changes; and provides transparency on investigative findings. I met Ms. Shihata during the first days of our three-year journey through the halls and complex courses at the University of Michigan Law School. During law school, Ms. Shihata was a star student. Ms. Shihata’s work ethic and notable acumen led to her outstanding academic performance. She graduated in the top two percent of her class and received the Bates Memorial Scholarship, the law school’s highest honor. Ms. Shihata was not only esteemed by the law school faculty and administration, her peers and colleagues respected and admired her. As a testament of her peers’ appreciation for her intellect and leadership, Ms. Shihata was selected to serve as the Editor-in-Chief (EIC) of the Michigan Law Review, one of the most coveted achievements for law students, where she managed a staff of approximately 100 students in publishing eight issues of the law journal each year and organized an annual symposium. Ms. Shihata was also a finalist in the Law School’s prestigious moot court competition.

2000 H STREET, N.W. ! WASHINGTON, DC 20052 2 Today, more than twenty years later, I continue to be impressed by Ms. Shihata’s work ethic, depth of character, and commitment to the foundational principles that have guided her service to the profession and the country. Based on my engagement with Ms. Shihata and my observations of her carrying out her professional duties, as well as engaging with peers and senior-ranking government officials over more than two decades, I believe that Ms. Shihata’s capabilities and background will enable her to effectively lead the DOI and serve the City of New York well. I currently serve as the Lyle T. Alverson Professor of Law at George Washington University Law School. In September of 2021, President Joseph R. Biden nominated me to serve as a Commissioner of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). In March of 2022, I was unanimously confirmed by the United States Senate. In my role as a CFTC Commissioner, I participated directly in decisions to advance enforcement matters from early-stage investigations through trials or settlement in matters that alleged violations of federal financial markets law and regulation. In June 2024, President Biden nominated me to serve as the Assistant Secretary for Financial Institutions at the United States Department of the Treasury (Treasury). Had I been confirmed, serving in Treasury would have expanded the scope of my duties, particularly duties related to enforcement of federal regulations. Prior to my service as an appointee in the Biden Administration, I served as a tenured law professor and Dean of Faculty Research at various institutions, including Emory University Law School and, Tulane University Law School. I began my law teaching career in the New York metropolitan area, where I taught law school courses for a decade and lived on the Upper West Side, Manhattan and Park Slope, Brooklyn. I have been a member of the New York State Bar since 2004 and prior to law school served as an analyst at Goldman Sachs and following law school as an associate at a New York based, large law firm and later as Vice President and Associate General Counsel at JP Morgan in New York City. .\, As a close friend of Ms. Shihata, I have had the privilege of witnessing her personal and professional growth throughout her career. Sitting in the courtroom during trials that she led early in her career at the U.S. Attorney’s office in the Eastern District of New York, it was clear that Ms. Shihata was not only effective in her representation, but her professionalism garnered the respect of her fellow federal prosecutors, opposing counsel, and the judges who presided over the trials that I observed. Ms. Shihata’s appointment as Chief of the Organized Crime and Gangs Section and Deputy Chief of the Public Integrity Section further evidence the broad support from peers and supervisors that Ms. Shihata enjoyed while serving as a federal prosecutor. Indeed, it is difficult to overstate Ms. Shihata’s talents and capabilities. In environments full of smart, seasoned lawyers, Ms. Shihata’s ability to navigate the complexities and intricacies of law and legal practice stands out. As a federal prosecutor, she has held powerful individuals accountable for victimizing the most vulnerable among us, whether they be celebrity musicians or law enforcement officers.

Let me say that again. I’m Council Member Jim Gennaro, Chair of the Committee on Environmental Protection and Waterfronts. like boating and that kind of thing. We’re just looking for a, you know, more full coverage like when it comes to testing, and we’re going to have some, you know, debate about that. I don’t think DEP is going to be crazy about it. I think some of the advocates are. And so, we’re going to have some fun today. Next Intro, Intro 795 would require Parks to install, replace, or upgrade 500 outdoor drinking fountains by 2035. This is Sandy Nurse’s bill. Such fountains would be required to have bottle filling stations and be accessible to people with disabilities. Additionally, Parks would be required to report the locations of the 500 fountains and assess the feasibility of year-round outdoor drinking fountains. Good afternoon, Chair Gennaro and members of the Committee. I’m Beth DeFalco, Deputy Commissioner for Public Affairs at DEP. Thank you for the opportunity to be here today to discuss Intros 730A, 804, and 795. I’ll take them in turn. Intro 730A is rooted in the shared priority, making sure New Yorkers have clear, timely information about water quality. There are a lot of reasons and ways to monitor and to receive timely information about what exactly is in our local waters. First and foremost is human health. The presence of bacteria from fecal matter, whether from storm runoff or untreated sewerage, and certain kinds of algae are potentially harmful to human health when people come into direct contact with water. Ecological health is another reason for robust water quality programs. The presence of excessive nitrogen or low oxygen levels or excessive amounts of certain algae can be harmful to plants and

creatures that live in our water bodies and that are essential for a balanced ecosystem. Finally, not only are clean beautiful water bodies a sign of a healthy environment, but we also recognize that there are important quality of life reasons to work toward that goal. Good water clarity is key to attracting people to our waterfronts and for the promotion of recreational activity where appropriate such as boating and site seeing. Recreation, as we know, is vitally important for maintaining vibrant, desirable communities where people want to visit, live and work. We look forward to arriving at legislation that accomplishes our shared goals of not just keeping the public informed and making sure that our local waters are as healthy, clean and as beautiful as possible. Regarding Intro 808 about light pollution: Intro 80–
[interposing] 804.

804, pardon me, 804. Intro 804 takes on an important issue, light pollution, and we support the goal of reducing unnecessary light in residential areas, particularly given the impacts of quality of life and public health. That said, we believe the bill needs more

clarity to be implementable. Right now, there are key terms that aren’t defined such as “other lighting.” It's also unclear whether the bill applies strictly to residential zones or extends into mixed use areas, which is a big distinction in New York City. There are also practical questions. The bill sets a 3,000 lumen limit, but doesn’t specify how that’s measured, whether it’s by fixture or by bulb, from what distance, from what direction, and it doesn’t address ambient light. In the City of New York, that can be very significant. Just as importantly, the bill doesn’t identify which agency would enforce this policy or how it would be paid for. This is not work that any city agency currently does. While we don’t believe that the bill is enforceable as it stands now, as always, we’re happy to work with the Council to help tighten the bill so it can achieve the goals in a clear and enforceable way. Regarding Intro 795: This speaks to something that we strongly agree with, making sure that New Yorkers have access to clean, free drinking water. However, DEP does have some concerns regarding the responsibilities and scope of this bill as it’s assigned to this agency regarding the 10 drinking

fountains. DEP doesn’t install or maintain any drinking fountains. It’s simply not part of our operational scope, and it’s not something that we’re well-suited to take on. In a non-park public place, fountains are typically installed and maintained by other entities, often private partners, and DEP does not have a role in those arrangements. The bill also doesn’t address ongoing maintenance which is critical. Installing a fountain is one thing. Keeping it clean, functional, and safe over time such that it would actually be used and served its intended purposes is where the real enduring work is. So, from our perspective, the bill needs clear assignment between its goals and the entities best-positioned to deliver on it, along with clarity on long-term responsibility. We’re committed to supporting the Council’s goals here, and we’re ready to help shape a path that works. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify and your continued partnership. We look forward to working on these.
Thank you. Sure, I just want to thank Beth, and please proceed with your testimony.

Thank you. Good afternoon, Chair Gennaro, members of the Environmental Protection and Waterfront Committee and members of City Council. I’m Mark Focht. I’m Acting First Deputy Commissioner of New York City Parks. Thank you for having us here today alongside our partners at DEP to discuss Intro 975 which would require New York City Parks to install, replace or upgrade 500 outdoor drinking fountains in various parks over the next nine years, with 300 required to take place in the next five years. NYC Parks maintains over 3,400 exterior drinking fountains throughout our parks and playgrounds, making us far and away the largest provider of clean drinking water for New Yorkers, and our dedicated staff works extremely hard to keep them in good working order. As a general practice, we incorporate new and replacement water fountains into the design of nearly all of our Parks renovation capital projects, making sure they are thoughtfully located to best serve park visitors, whether it’s used by kids at playgrounds or a jogger taking a break. In advance of every winter, the majority of those outdoor drinking fountains need to be winterized, meaning manually drained and

deactivated by our dedicated trade staff to avoid damage to the subsurface infrastructure from freezing pipes. As we speak, those same trades are in the process of reactivating our thousands of water features throughout the park system, including our drinking fountains, to make sure that New Yorkers can enjoy them as the temperatures rise. Whenever new or upgraded drinking fountains are installed as part of larger Parks capital projects, depending on the individual site needs and project budget, we install both ADA-compliant drinking fountains and bottle fillers to sites when feasible. As a general practice, our park’s water fountains are located near well use features and amenities within parks such a children’s play area, seating areas, or athletic fields and ports to make sure the fountains are available where park users need them most. There are several different standard models we utilize for drinking fountains in parks, running from high-low drinking fountains which offer access of two different heights to standalone down-flowing bottle fillers, some of which include an additional spigot and bowl at the base for dog owners to utilize. We are very committed to increasing the amount of water

fountains accessible in our parks and are proud to share that in the five-year period from fiscal year 21 to fiscal year 25 we installed a total of 527 drinking fountains and bottle fillers, including free-standing units, as well as those installed on the sides of our public restrooms. Turning to the legislation today– as you may be aware, NYC Parks is already working to comply with Local Law 93 passed by Council last year which mandated the installation of drinking fountains within parks over the next 10 years. Through this effort, we are seeking to identify every opportunity to add or improve drinking fountains throughout our portfolio. As such, while we share Council’s support to expanding access to drinking water, we believe that Introduction 795 is largely duplicative of the recently enacted law, the language which was negotiated jointly between Council and the administration to ensure an appropriate and reasonable approach to improving public access to water fountains, a goal we all share. Thank you for allowing us to testify before you today and for your continued advocacy and support for parks. Certainly pleased to answer any questions you may have.
